title: Beshalach: the long way round (Exodus 13:17)
hookLine: God leads them away from the short road lest they see war and turn back
carry: the long way can be kinder

lines: THE ROAD THAT MAKES YOU TURN BACK.
cards: Open a map app and it hands you the fastest route, down to the minute. It doesn't know you hate that interchange.

It doesn't know you've only just learned to drive, or that the quick road runs past the house of someone you can't face yet. Sometimes the shortest road is the one most likely to make you turn around.
The Israelites are free. They're standing at the edge of Egypt, and the quickest road to the promised land runs straight along the coast.
A new portion begins here, and the very first thing it says is that God doesn't take it.

teach.b: The portion is called Beshalach, from its first phrase: when Pharaoh had let the people go.
The short way, the verse says, was the way of the land of the Philistines, along the sea. It was near.

teach.h: LEST THEY SEE WAR AND TURN BACK.
teach.b: And God led them another way, and the Torah gives the reason in God's own words: "Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt." Repent here means change their minds.
People who had been slaves the day before weren't ready for a battle. One look at an army and Egypt would have seemed safe again.
So God sends them the long way, through the wilderness, toward the sea, chosen for their sake, not for speed. The medieval philosopher Maimonides leaned on this verse.
It shows, he said, how God works with human nature rather than against it.
People can't leap from one way of life to its opposite overnight, so the Torah leads them gently, step by step, the way you'd lead someone who's frightened.

teach.h: THE LONG WAY CAN BE KINDER.
teach.b: He even used the verse to explain why the long years in the wilderness were needed: to raise a generation used to freedom. Notice what the long way isn't. It isn't avoidance.
The sea is still coming, and so are hard days. It's a road sized to who you are right now, so you don't give up before you arrive.

how: Beshalach is read in synagogue in winter, on the Shabbat called Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song, because it contains the Song at the Sea, which the congregation often stands for.

games.q: you're leading a people who were slaves yesterday. the short road home runs past an army. what does the story say God does?

lead them the long way, through the wilderness.

games.why: the long way, toward the sea, lest they see war and turn back. the route is sized to who they are.

practice: Think of something you're trying to change, a habit, a relationship, a part of yourself, and ask whether you've been taking the shortest road, all at once, and turning back every time it gets hard.
Now picture a longer road instead: a smaller first step, a slower pace you could actually keep. Don't decide everything; just see the longer road, and notice whether it feels kinder.
